edited_rows.rationale: The composition opens with a thanksgiving vow, “I will give you thanks with my whole heart” (web:Ps.138.1), and closes with a confident petition, “Don’t forsake the works of your own hands” (web:Ps.138.8), an envelope from vow to petition that runs across only 8 verses -- within the short-psalm threshold for a whole-psalm row. The middle sets direct address aside for the kings’ report (web:Ps.138.4-5) and Yahweh’s care for the lowly (web:Ps.138.6), a third-person interval framed by direct address on both sides (web:Ps.138.4, web:Ps.138.7), before web:Ps.138.7 returns to address Yahweh directly through the close; the interval develops the opening vow rather than opening an independently marked strophe (no selah, no vocative reset, no genre-label shift inside the body).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting after web:Ps.138.4’s shift from personal thanksgiving to the kings’ response was considered, but web:Ps.138.5 continues the same third-person report about Yahweh’s ways without a vocative reset strong enough to carry a strophe break in a psalm this short.

Or where could I flee from your presence?” (web:Ps.139.7), surveying heaven, Sheol, and the wings of the dawn (web:Ps.139.8-10) before closing on darkness and light (web:Ps.139.11-12). An anaphoric “gam” (גם, “even/also”) opens both web:Ps.139.10 and web:Ps.139.12 at the consonantal (skeleton) tier, tying the unit's middle to its own close rather than to the prior movement's close at web:Ps.139.6.

The strophe turns to a rhetorical meditation without changing addressee, מָה אָ֭דָם (oshb:Ps.144.3), “Yahweh, what is man, that you care for him?” (web:Ps.144.3), resolved in the breath-and-shadow figure of “Man is like a breath. His days are like a shadow that passes away.” (web:Ps.144.4). It closes before the fresh imperative petition that opens web:Ps.144.5.

The rescued-king motif also answers Ps 18's own close naming David (web:Ps.18.50).
